opus-5.5.text:
I think of it really as a two-way street, and honestly the direction that excites me most these days is the one people talk about less: science for AI. A lot of the ideas that ended up being useful in machine learning came straight out of physics. If you look at things like variational inference, that's basically free energy minimization from statistical mechanics. Diffusion models are non-equilibrium thermodynamics. Equivariance, the idea that you should build symmetries into your neural networks, comes from how physicists think about gauge theories and group representations. So a big part of my career has been saying: physicists have spent a century figuring out how to describe the world compactly, with symmetries and conservation laws, so let's take those tools and use them to build better learning machines.

Then there's the other direction, AI for science, which is where I've been putting more and more of my energy. The way I see it, we're at a moment where the tools are finally good enough that you can actually accelerate discovery in a real way, in materials, in chemistry, in drug design. Molecules are a beautiful example because they obey the laws of physics exactly, so you can bring all those inductive biases, the symmetries, the equivariance, into the models, and then they become much more data efficient. And you need that, because in science data is expensive. Every data point might be a wet lab experiment or a very expensive quantum chemistry simulation.

What I find really interesting is that the loop is starting to close. You have generative models proposing candidate molecules or materials, simulators or experiments evaluating them, and the results feeding back into the model. That's essentially an active learning or experimental design loop, and if you do it well you're not just predicting, you're actually searching the space of possible matter in a smart way. That's something I care about a lot, also for very practical reasons: think about climate, about new battery materials, about capturing carbon. These are problems where better materials can make an enormous difference, and I think AI can really speed up the process of finding them.

So if I had to summarize my contribution, I'd say I've tried to be a bit of a bridge. I was trained as a physicist, I wandered into machine learning, and now I'm sort of bringing machine learning back to the physical sciences. And I think the most interesting work happens exactly at that boundary, where the two communities actually have to learn each other's language.

r001.rationale: The response describes growing activity in AI for science and says the discovery loop is starting to close, but it does not characterize AI for science or science for AI as an emerging discipline.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of it as a two-way street, and honestly the direction that excites me most right now is AI for science, because that's where I've spent the last several years.

My background is in physics, and for a long time my work in machine learning was really about importing ideas from physics into AI. Things like symmetries and equivariance, where you build the structure of the problem directly into the model so it doesn't have to learn from scratch that the laws of nature don't care which way you rotate your coordinate system. Group-equivariant networks came out of that line of thinking, and they turned out to be useful well beyond physics, in medical imaging, in molecules, in anything with geometric structure. So that's the science-for-AI side: physics gave us inductive biases that made models more data efficient and more trustworthy.

But at some point I realized the arrow should flip. The deep problems humanity faces, in energy, in materials, in drug discovery, in climate, are fundamentally problems of simulation and search over enormous spaces. Quantum chemistry is a great example. We know the equations, the Schrödinger equation has been around for a century, but solving it accurately for anything beyond a handful of atoms is computationally hopeless. So the question becomes: can we train models that learn to approximate those solutions, and then use them to search over millions of candidate molecules or materials far faster than any lab or any supercomputer running the exact calculation? That's what I've been pushing on, and it's why I eventually moved into building a company around it, because I think the real impact comes from actually putting these tools into the hands of chemists and materials scientists.

What I'd say my contribution is, if I'm being honest, is less any single method and more an insistence that these two worlds belong together. Machine learning people tend to treat science as just another dataset, and scientists tend to treat machine learning as a black box they don't trust. I've tried to sit in the middle and say: the physics tells you what structure to build in, and the learning tells you how to fill in what you can't derive. When you get that balance right, you get models that generalize, that respect conservation laws, that a scientist can actually believe. And I think over the next decade that combination is going to compress the timeline for discovery in a way that's hard to overstate.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI for science and science for AI as a two-way combination and says its impact will grow over the next decade, but does not clearly characterize it as an emerging discipline.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a two-way exchange. In one direction, science gives us principles for building AI. Physics, for example, teaches us to think about symmetry: what should change when you rotate a system, and what should stay the same? If you build that structure into a model, it doesn’t have to learn it all from data. That can make learning much more efficient.

In the other direction, AI gives us new tools for doing science. We can build models that approximate expensive simulations, explore possible molecules or materials, and help decide which experiment to do next. But there, predicting well is only part of the problem. You also want to know when the model is uncertain and whether it remains reliable outside the conditions it was trained on.

So I see my contribution at that interface: using scientific structure to build better learning methods, and then using those methods to help us investigate scientific questions. What interests me is the feedback between the two.

r001.rationale: The response describes a two-way exchange between science and AI, but does not characterize it as an emerging discipline.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a two-way street. My background is in physics, and that has shaped how I approach machine learning. In physics, you look for symmetries, you think about uncertainty, and you try to find a simple description of a complicated system. Those are very useful principles for building AI as well.

Then, in the other direction, you can use machine learning to help solve scientific problems. For me, a particularly interesting area is molecules: how do you build models that understand their geometry and can predict their properties? That brings the two directions together, because the physics tells you something about the structure your model should have, and the model helps you explore systems that would otherwise be very expensive to study.

So I see my contribution as building that bridge. You bring scientific structure into machine learning, and then use those methods to give something back to science.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI for science and science for AI as a two-way bridge, but does not characterize it as an emerging discipline.
